Trail Notes — Packing Guides

HOW TO PACK FOR A DOG-FRIENDLY DAY HIKE

5 min read · Updated June 2026

Day Hike Packing All Seasons

Most dog owners underprepare for their first trail day — no bowl, no shade plan, maybe a leash and some water they'd planned to share. By the third hike they've overcorrected: a 40-pound pack for a 4-mile loop. The right kit sits between those two. The shape of the outing determines what you need far more than the breed of your dog or the season alone.

Start With the Outing, Not the Dog

Under 4 miles round trip: you need water and a collapsible bowl, a couple of waste bags, and paw balm if the trail runs hot or rocky. That's it. A 60-pound dog on a 3-mile shaded loop in October needs almost nothing beyond what you're already carrying for yourself. Four to 8 miles changes the math: add a small trail first aid kit (wound wrap, tick tool, antiseptic wipe), an extra 16oz of water per dog, and something temperature-appropriate — a cooling bandana in summer, paw wax for salted winter roads. Over 8 miles, your dog carries their own load. A healthy dog weighing 40 pounds or more can comfortably carry 15 to 20 percent of their body weight. That's where the pack conversation starts.

Hydration: More Than You Think

Dogs need roughly 1 ounce of water per pound of body weight per day at rest. On a warm, active trail day, that figure can double. For a 50-pound dog on a 6-mile summer hike, you should plan for at least 48 ounces of water beyond what you'd otherwise carry — and more if the trail is exposed or the dog is a high-output breed. Collapsible silicone bowls fold to under an inch and weigh almost nothing. Use them instead of letting a dog drink from shared trail water sources, which can carry Giardia at concentrations that hit dogs harder than most people expect. On hot days or for dogs that pant hard, electrolyte powder formulated for dogs (not humans — the sodium ratios are different) makes a real difference over 5 or more miles.

Paw Care Before and After

Pavement burns at around 125°F when the air temperature is 85°F. Seven-second test: place your palm on the ground. If you can't hold it for 7 seconds, the ground will burn your dog's pads. Dirt trail absorbs heat differently and cools faster, but sharp rocks and gravel cause cuts regardless of temperature. Apply a thin layer of paw wax before hot or rocky sections — it creates a barrier without reducing traction the way booties sometimes do for dogs not trained in them. Check pads after every hike. Cuts between toes are easy to miss and quick to get infected on subsequent outings.

The First Aid Minimum

A trail kit is not a home kit. It needs to be light enough to actually come with you. The essential list: self-adhesive wound wrap (not standard bandage — it sticks to itself without tape), one antiseptic wipe packet, a tick removal tool (not tweezers — the right tool removes the head cleanly), a small square of foil emergency blanket in case of shock, and a 6-inch strip of vet tape. That's the field kit. It weighs 8 ounces total. Everything else — antihistamine tablets, eye wash, gauze pads — gets added on longer or more remote trips, not on day hikes within cell range. The rule is: carry what you'll actually use before you can get the dog to a vet.

What Goes in the Dog's Pack vs. Your Pack

Once your dog is old enough (12 to 18 months, depending on breed), healthy, and trail-fit, they can start carrying their own weight. Start at 10 percent body weight, build toward 20 percent over several outings. Put food, water, and waste bags in the dog's pack — these are the weights a dog is physically suited to distribute. Keep the first aid kit, the emergency foil, and anything you'd need to access quickly in your pack. A dog pack that fits badly is worse than no dog pack: it shifts forward on downhills, restricts shoulder movement, and creates hotspots under the straps after 3 or 4 miles. Measure the girth (just behind the front legs) and back length before ordering.

Cleanup Starts at the Trailhead

The best trail dog owners have a ritual they run at the car. Waste gets bagged on trail — always. At the trailhead parking lot, paws get wiped before the dog gets back in. The car mat goes in before the dog. The leash clips to the door handle while paws are drying. This three-minute sequence is the difference between a clean car and a car that smells like six months of trail mud. Compostable waste bags compact enough to clip to a pack ring are worth the small price premium over grocery bags — the volume difference is negligible and they hold up under wet conditions.

Temperature Considerations

Anything over 80°F: cooling bandana soaked in cold water, at least 30% more water than usual, and plan for 20% less distance than you'd cover in mild weather. The dog will tell you when they're done — excessive panting, lagging behind, seeking shade — but by that point they're already running hot. Under 45°F: paw wax to protect against salt and ice crystals, and a coat for short-haired, small, or lean-body dogs. Rain changes the game on leash grip: a waterproof leash won't get stiff and heavy, and it actually dries out between uses rather than staying damp in your car for three days.

Day hike packing is one of those skills that self-corrects fast. The first time you arrive at a trailhead without a bowl and watch your dog try to drink from your hand, you don't forget the bowl again. After a few outings you're running through the list in your head on the way out the door — water, bowl, bags, balm, first aid — and it takes about forty-five seconds. That's where you want to be.
